"You winced when I said Friday," Himani said, stirring her coffee at the office pantry. "Is Friday bad?"
Pallavi laughed. "No, no. I bit my tongue on the biscuit a second ago."
"Oh! I thought you were dreading the deadline."
"I might be, a little," Pallavi admitted. "But that wince was the tongue."
Himani nodded. "I keep doing that, taking a face and building a story on it. Last week I decided the client was annoyed because he frowned, and it turned out the sun was in his eyes."
"So you ask now?"
"I try. A face is one clue. The words and the situation are others. So, Friday: is it okay for you?"
"Friday is fine. I'd just like the draft by Thursday evening."
"Done."

qa.q: What did Pallavi bite on?
qa.a: Pallavi bit their tongue on the biscuit.

qa.q: What did Himani first think Pallavi's wince meant, and what was actually behind it?
qa.a: Himani thought Pallavi was dreading Friday's deadline, but the wince came from a bitten tongue, though Pallavi admits to maybe being a little worried too.

qa.q: What could Himani keep doing to read faces better?
qa.a: She could treat a face as one clue among words and situation and check with the person, as she did by asking about Friday.

qa.q: How might Pallavi feel about being asked instead of assumed?
qa.a: Pallavi seems comfortable, since Pallavi laughed and explained, and could also raise the real worry about the draft.

grounding: Himani treats Pallavi's wince as one clue and checks it, learning the face had a different cause.

passage: I'm Pradeep, and I used to be very sure of my reading of faces. In my first year as a site engineer, my supervisor Chaitanya frowned deeply through a whole safety briefing. I decided he was furious with the team and spent the day tense, double-checking everything. That evening I finally asked, "Was there something wrong with how we did the site checks?" He looked startled. "No, the projector was too bright and I forgot my glasses. I'm sorry, I must have looked terrible." I laughed out of pure relief. Since then I treat a scowl or a grin as a guess. I look at what the person says, what's happening around them, and if it matters, I ask them kindly.

qa.q: What job did Pradeep have in the first year?
qa.a: Pradeep was a site engineer.

qa.q: What did Pradeep feel about Chaitanya's frown, and what was actually going on?
qa.a: Pradeep felt tense, thinking Chaitanya was furious, but the frown was caused by the bright projector and his forgotten glasses.

qa.q: What could Pradeep do the next time someone frowns during a meeting?
qa.a: Pradeep could hold the guess loosely, notice the words and situation, and ask kindly if it matters.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya have felt when Pradeep asked about the site checks?
qa.a: Chaitanya was startled and apologetic, since he hadn't realised how his face looked to the team.

grounding: Pradeep learns to treat a frown as one clue and to check with the person.

passage:
Nursing supervisor's note, medical ward, night shift.
Amandeep, our new staff nurse, is twenty-four and quick to learn. Tonight she came to me upset: the elderly man in bed 7 had scowled at her all evening, and she was sure he was angry with her for something. I asked what else she had noticed. She thought for a moment. He had been squinting at the clock. He hadn't touched his dinner. His voice was polite when he spoke. Together we went to his bed, and Amandeep asked gently, "Uncle, is anything bothering you?" He said his reading glasses were at home and the lights hurt his eyes, and his back ached from the bed. Not anger at all. Amandeep adjusted his pillows and dimmed the light over his bed, and his face relaxed. Afterwards she said, "I nearly avoided him all night." I told her a face is one clue; the words and the situation are the others.
— Salma

qa.q: What did the man in bed 7 say was bothering him?
qa.a: His reading glasses were at home, the lights hurt his eyes, and his back ached from the bed.

qa.q: What was Amandeep feeling when she came to her supervisor?
qa.a: She was upset and anxious, sure the patient's scowl meant he was angry with her.

qa.q: What helped Amandeep read the patient's scowl correctly?
qa.a: Looking at other clues like the squinting and polite voice, and then asking him gently instead of avoiding him.

qa.q: How did the patient experience the evening before Amandeep asked?
qa.a: He was uncomfortable, with the lights hurting his eyes and his back aching, which caused the scowl.

grounding: Shows a young professional learning to treat a scowl as one clue among many and checking with the person.

passage:
Thursday.
In today's budget meeting, when I explained why my project needed two more weeks, Bhupen grinned. A wide grin, right in the middle of my worst slide. I felt my face go hot. Was he mocking me? He's senior and I'm the new one; it would make sense. I spent the rest of the meeting half-listening, rehearsing a cold reply.
After the meeting I made myself go to his desk instead of stewing. "Bhupen, when I asked for the extra two weeks, you grinned. Did I say something funny?"
He looked horrified. "No! I grin when I'm nervous. I was worried the director would say no, and I was about to ask for the same thing for my team."
We ended up writing a joint request. The director approved both.
Note to self: a grin can be nerves, not a joke. Ask first. Fume later, if needed.
— Francis

qa.q: How many more weeks did Francis's project need?
qa.a: Two more weeks.

qa.q: What was Francis feeling when Bhupen grinned?
qa.a: Francis felt embarrassed and hurt, face going hot, suspecting Bhupen was mocking.

qa.q: What did Francis do that turned things around?
qa.a: Francis asked Bhupen directly and calmly about the grin instead of stewing or replying coldly.

qa.q: What was Bhupen actually feeling when he grinned?
qa.a: He was nervous, worried the director would say no, because he was about to make the same request for his team.

grounding: Shows a young professional treating a colleague's grin as one clue, holding the guess loosely and checking with the person.

Tenzin: was I?? 😅
Tanvir: yes. I thought you hated the proposal. I nearly stopped halfway
Tenzin: oh no. no no
Tenzin: I was concentrating really hard on the numbers. and the projector light was right in my eyes
Tanvir: ohh. that makes sense
Tenzin: also I had a headache since lunch
Tanvir: I built a whole story from one face lol

Tanvir: phew. ok. thanks for telling me
Tenzin: next time just message me during. I'll uncrinkle my face 🙂

qa.q: What was in Tenzin's eyes during the presentation?
qa.a: The projector light.

qa.q: What was Tanvir feeling during the presentation?
qa.a: Tanvir was anxious and unsure, thinking Tenzin hated the proposal and nearly stopping halfway.

qa.q: What did Tanvir do that was wise?
qa.a: Tanvir asked Tenzin about the scowl afterwards instead of assuming, and learned the real reasons.

qa.q: How did Tenzin actually see the proposal?
qa.a: Tenzin thought it was good and even wrote down two questions for the next day.

grounding: Shows a young professional treating a colleague's scowl as one clue and checking, since the same face can come from several states.

passage:
The power had gone out again in Keerthana's tailoring shop near the Kumbakonam bus stand, so the two women worked by the light from the doorway. When Keerthana read out the wedding order, forty blouses in nine days, Hafsa winced and pressed her lips together.
Keerthana's first thought was that Hafsa hated the deadline, or hated being asked at all. Then she noticed Hafsa's hand drifting to her jaw, and that her voice, when she said, "Fine, we can manage," sounded steady enough.
Keerthana put the order book down. "That face could mean a few things. Is it the order, or is something hurting?"
Hafsa laughed, then winced again. "A back tooth. Since yesterday. The order is fine, akka."
Keerthana wrote the dentist's timings on the back of the order slip and pushed it across the table.

qa.q: How many blouses did the wedding order ask for?
qa.a: The wedding order asked for forty blouses in nine days.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling when Hafsa winced at the order?
qa.a: Keerthana felt uneasy, guessing Hafsa resented the tight deadline; but the hand at the jaw and the steady voice made her doubt that reading, so she held it loosely and asked.

qa.q: Which choice worked here, and why?
qa.a: Asking an open question worked, because Keerthana named more than one possible reason instead of acting on her first guess, and so she learned about the tooth.

qa.q: How might Hafsa have felt if Keerthana had treated her as unwilling?
qa.a: Hafsa could have felt misjudged and hurt, since she was ready to take on the order and was only in pain.

grounding: A reader treats a wince as one clue alongside voice, words and situation, and checks with the person instead of trusting the first guess.
